objects.name: CTFT Project
objects.description: Capture-The-Flag Techniques - an ontology of CTF solving behaviour. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC and CWE as per-entry anchors; not a parallel ATT&CK. Generalized from FOM.

objects.name: AI / ML
objects.description: Secrets inside models/prompts/serialized artifacts and their extraction. (HTB: AI-ML)

objects.name: Blockchain
objects.description: On-chain/contract concealment and EVM-level recovery. (HTB: Blockchain)

objects.name: Cloud
objects.description: Cloud misconfiguration concealment and enumeration-based recovery. (HTB: Cloud)

objects.name: Coding / Programming Puzzle
objects.description: Challenges where the flag is gated behind a programming or algorithmic problem: an esoteric language, a time-bounded algorithm, a scripted marathon of protocol rounds, a polyglot/code-golf constraint, or a constraint-satisfaction puzzle solvable with symbolic execution. (HTB: Coding)

objects.name: Cryptography
objects.description: Deliberately weakened or layered crypto and its cryptanalysis. (HTB: Crypto)

objects.name: Forensics
objects.description: Challenges where the flag survives in an artifact but not in plain sight: tampered file signatures, slack and unallocated space, falsified timestamps, alternate data streams, memory images, packet captures and unusual encodings. Recovery is structural — read what the container actually is, not what it claims to be. (HTB: Forensics)

objects.name: Full Pwn / Multi-Stage
objects.description: Challenges that require a complete host or infrastructure compromise across multiple stages — reconnaissance, foothold, and privilege escalation — before the flag is reachable. The flag is reachable only at the end of the chain, so no single technique solves the challenge. (HTB: Fullpwn)

objects.name: Game / Protocol Automation (GamePwn)
objects.description: Challenges built around a game binary or networked game server. The author hides the flag behind game mechanics that require automation, binary patching, memory manipulation, AI defeat, or protocol sequence exploitation rather than raw exploit code. (HTB: GamePwn)

objects.name: Hardware
objects.description: Hiding data in embedded interfaces/signals and physically extracting it. (HTB: Hardware)

objects.name: ICS / SCADA
objects.description: Industrial-protocol register/memory hiding and protocol-level extraction. (HTB: ICS)

objects.name: IoT / Embedded
objects.description: Hiding/recovering flags inside internet-connected devices: consumer firmware images and their embedded web stacks, IoT messaging brokers (MQTT/CoAP), on-board serial consoles, short-range device radio (Zigbee/BLE/sub-GHz), and the emulation of embedded binaries (MIPS/ARM). Distinct from HWR (electronic badges without a network story), ICS (industrial control systems) and SDR (generic RF signal puzzles): the subject here is the consumer/connected device and its firmware-to-cloud chain. (HTB: Misc (IoT))

objects.name: Jail / Sandbox Escape
objects.description: Challenges where the author constructs a restricted execution environment — a language-level sandbox, a limited shell, or an OS/kernel isolation boundary — to prevent direct flag access. Solvers must find a path out of the confinement. (HTB: Misc (Jail))

objects.name: Mobile
objects.description: Secrets concealed in mobile apps and runtime, recovered statically/dynamically. (HTB: Mobile)

objects.name: Network
objects.description: Hiding flags behind network discovery, sniffing, tunneling and protocol-barrier puzzles. (HTB: Misc (Network))

objects.name: OSINT
objects.description: Information dispersed across public sources and correlated back together. (HTB: OSINT)

objects.name: Binary Exploitation
objects.description: Hiding flags behind memory-corruption gates and constrained runtime puzzles. (HTB: Pwn)

objects.name: Reverse Engineering
objects.description: Concealing logic in binaries/bytecode and reconstructing it. (HTB: Reversing)

objects.name: Software-Defined Radio
objects.description: Hiding data in RF captures and modulated signals, and recovering it through SDR demodulation and decoding. Split from HWR (Hardware), which keeps embedded-device and physical-interface concealment. The barrier can sit at any layer of the receive chain: - finding the signal in a live spectrum; - reading an unlabelled IQ file (format, sample rate, centre); - identifying the modulation; - slicing on-off-keyed symbols and undoing a line code (Manchester, PWM, PPM); - running a standard protocol decoder (pager, packet, ADS-B). IoT protocol stacks with pairing keys (Zigbee/BLE) stay in IOT; tones already in an audio file stay in STE. Recovery is receive-only. (HTB: Hardware)

objects.name: Steganography
objects.description: Challenges where a payload is embedded inside an otherwise valid carrier — image bitplanes, audio spectrograms, metadata containers, invisible characters or the wording of a text — so that the carrier stays openable and looks untouched. Recovery works on the carrier's representation rather than its content. (HTB: Forensics/Misc (Stego))

objects.name: CTFTTE-CLD-001 - Misconfigured object-storage exposure
objects.description: The flag object sits in a world-readable or weakly-named bucket the author assumes is private. The weakness is in the access policy, not in the data: an ACL or bucket policy grants read to a principal set that includes anonymous callers, or the object itself is public while the bucket is not. Nothing in the traffic resembles an attack — an unauthenticated request returns the flag. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Listable bucket. Anonymous callers may list the bucket, so object names are handed over and the flag object downloads directly. - Readable objects, denied listing. The list operation is refused while individual objects are served: the exposure is complete, only the index is missing. - Guessable name. The prompt or a leaked artefact supplies a keyword instead of a name, and the bucket name is that keyword plus a short, predictable qualifier. - Versioned storage. A deleted object survives as a non-current version that stays readable. - Storage as a carrier. The exposed objects hold a further artefact (source tree, repository, configuration) whose history or companion files contain credentials, so the bucket is the entry point to a second weakness rather than the flag itself. Boundary: when the grant is scoped to any authenticated principal of the provider, the exposure is credential-gated and no longer anonymous — that belongs to the over-permissive-access pairs.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CLD-001 - Enumerate and list public buckets
objects.description: Enumerate bucket names and list/download objects anonymously. 1. Normalise the identity. Object-store name alone, DNS name, or the bucket segment inside a URL path — drop the scheme, the storage URI prefix and any region suffix. When only a keyword is given, expand it with the qualifiers authors actually use (visibility, environment, role, year) before reaching for a dictionary. 2. Resolve region and endpoint before judging permissions. An unsigned HEAD on the bucket root usually advertises the region in a response header even when the body is refused, and a redirect is a wrong-region answer rather than a denial. Retrying against the regional endpoint is the most commonly wasted hour in this technique. 3. List anonymously. Issue the list-objects call unsigned, with pagination, and no request signing of any kind. 4. When the listing is refused, change the endpoint, not the target. Two fallbacks carry most of the weight: the versioned listing (it also names deleted objects and their version identifiers) and a direct object read on guessed keys, since a read-only grant often coexists with a denied list. 5. Treat every object as an artefact. Download the set, match the expected answer format, then follow what each object is: an archive, a source tree or a repository can hold credentials in its history or companion files, which pivots the challenge to the over-permissive-access pair — only with explicit authorization. Signatures to expect: success on the listing; a refused listing with object bodies still served; a redirect that encodes a region mismatch; a provider error code for a missing bucket; a disabled or suspended storage account; a blanket refusal (private, or a grant scoped to authenticated callers).
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CLD-007 - Cloud NoSQL-store misconfiguration
objects.description: A document or key-value store holds the flag and the misconfiguration is in the data plane, not in an object bucket: an endpoint that answers without authentication, a key that acts as the store's administrative principal, or a grant broad enough that enumerating databases and collections is itself the solve. Nothing resembles an injection — the store simply answers a request it should have refused. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Open endpoint. The data-plane endpoint accepts unauthenticated reads — sometimes only for metadata (database and collection names) and not for the documents themselves. - Administrative key in an artefact. A connection string or account key in a configuration, a bundle or a log grants the store's primary principal; the request must then be signed with that key rather than sent as a bearer token, and the signature recipe is the whole obstacle. - Narrow but sufficient grant. The identity may read one container only, so listing fails while a guessed document identifier succeeds. - Query surface over a plain read. The store's query language is reachable through a portal or a proxy, so the answer requires building the right query instead of reading a known identifier. - Compatibility layer. The store is reachable through a protocol emulation (a document API, a Mongo-compatible endpoint), and the flag is found with a client for that protocol rather than the provider's own. - Snapshot or change feed. An export, backup or change feed in a second service retains records the live store has already purged. Boundary: object storage rather than a database API belongs to the object-storage pair; a store reached with a leaked session token rather than a store credential belongs to the session-material pair.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CLD-007 - Enumerate and query exposed cloud databases
objects.description: Separate the two questions the store answers differently — what exists and what may I read — then build the request the store actually accepts. 1. Identify the API surface. A document API, a key-value API and a Mongo-compatible endpoint answer different paths with different authentication. Read the endpoint's error body before trying payloads: a version or api-version complaint names the protocol you must speak. 2. Establish the authentication model. Either the request carries a bearer token for the store's own audience, or it is signed with the account key (a date, a version, a resource and a signature over a canonical string). The signed form fails with a signature error rather than an authorisation error — that difference tells you which model is in play. 3. Enumerate metadata first. Listing databases and collections is a separate permission from reading documents; a successful metadata listing maps the space even when document reads are refused. 4. Read by identifier when listing is refused. Use the identifiers the narrative supplies and the conventions a store's own tooling would produce (partition keys, container names, well-known record identifiers) instead of blind brute force. 5. Query when the surface is a query language. A portal or proxy that exposes queries wants a query, not a path: learn the shape from one benign response, then constrain the next request. 6. Follow the data out of the store. A snapshot, export or change feed in a second service may retain records the live store has purged — check the artefact trail before concluding the store is decoy. Signatures to expect: metadata success with document reads refused; a signature-mismatch error naming the canonical pieces the service expects; a document read succeeding on a guessed identifier; a partition key error that reveals the schema; a version header echoed back with the accepted value.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CLD-008 - Azure management-plane misconfiguration
objects.description: The flag sits behind the management plane — the subscription's control API, the tenant directory, or a resource whose data plane is only reachable after a control-plane action. The challenge hands over something that authenticates (a service-principal secret, a user account, a certificate, an instance metadata endpoint, a cached session) and the configuration intends that principal to be narrower than it is: an over-broad role assignment, a directory role granted to a guest, a delegation that reaches another subscription, or a control-plane action that executes code on a resource. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Credential in an artefact. Client identifier plus secret or certificate in a configuration, a pipeline variable, a bundle or a log; resolving the tenant and subscription identifiers is the first move, not the last. - Instance metadata reachable. From a workload, or through a server-side request forgery, the metadata service mints a token for whatever resource the caller names — so the plane reached is chosen by the solver, not by the application. - Broad directory role. The principal reads or modifies directory objects, which exposes further credentials, applications, service principals and group memberships. - Control plane as execution. An action that runs a command or a script on a resource turns a read-looking grant into code execution on a host, with the output returned by the same API. - Cross-subscription reach. A grant at a management-group or root scope, or a guest principal with directory-wide read, exposes subscriptions the narrative never mentions. - Plane as a doorway. The credential is valid for the control plane, and the flag is in a resource's data plane (storage, vault, database, container registry) reached only after discovery, chaining into those pairs. Boundary: with no credential at all the challenge is anonymous exposure; with a store-scoped key it is the storage pair; with token material that must be re-audienced it is the session-material pair. Here the material authenticates to a control API.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CLD-008 - Enumerate Azure AD/VM/storage from credentials
objects.description: Ask the plane what the identity can do before asking it for anything, and descend one scope at a time: tenant → subscription → resource group → resource → data plane. 1. Normalise the credential. Separate what is present — client identifier with secret or certificate, user account, cached session file, metadata endpoint, raw token. Resolve the tenant (a domain name in the prompt is not a tenant identifier) and note the client identifier, because it decides which flows the endpoint accepts. 2. Establish the identity from the plane itself. One read of the signed-in principal, the token's own claims, or the caller-identity API answers who is acting. Do this before enumerating, so every later result is attributable. 3. Enumerate the reachable scopes, not just the current one. List every subscription and tenant the identity can see, then resource groups and resources within them. Delegation and management-group grants surface here and nowhere else. 4. Read the authorisation layer, not only the inventory. Role assignments and directory roles explain why a resource is reachable and point at the next hop: a principal with a role on another scope, an application holding a secret, a group whose membership can be read. 5. Prefer the read that proves the claim. Where the story says a resource is reachable, the evidence is the read that only an authorised principal can perform — not a dump of everything visible. 6. Use control-plane execution only when the objective demands it, and gate it. Actions that run a command on a resource change state; state the exact action and expected output before running it, and prefer a read-only alternative when the flag is data. 7. Follow the plane into the data plane. A resource's own API (storage, vault, database, registry, cluster) is a second authorisation check; the control-plane grant does not guarantee it. Signatures to expect: a token whose audience names the plane you need; a subscription list longer than the story implies; a role assignment at a parent scope explaining an otherwise surprising read; a resource that answers on the control plane but refuses its data plane (a second grant is missing); an execution action returning output instead of a status.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CLD-009 - Delegated sign-in session material exposed
objects.description: What the challenge hands over is not a password but session material: a refresh token, a device-code grant, a primary refresh token, a cached token file, a client secret, or an external assertion. The article the player holds is opaque, often expired, and its audience — not the login — decides which plane it opens. The author counts on the player either refusing to look inside the artefact or treating "the token has expired" as the end of the path. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Cached token store. A profile directory, an SDK cache or a CI secret holds an access token whose audience names a management plane the narrative never mentions. - Renewal credential only. Just the refresh token is supplied; one token request mints an access token for a resource of the solver's choosing, so the apparent absence of a usable token is the trick. - Device-code grant. The prompt supplies a code to redeem, or a retrieval endpoint is reachable; completing the flow yields a delegated identity whose scopes exceed the story. - Client family crossing audiences. The same refresh token reaches several first-party resources because the requesting client belongs to a family allowed to do so — the scope string, not the user, is the lever. - Session material needing import. Cookie or primary-refresh-token material must be placed in a client's expected form before the token endpoint accepts it. - Federated assertion. An external OIDC token is trusted by a workload identity federation object; only the exchange step separates the player from a cloud token. Boundary: a user password belongs to the credential-access pairs; a correctly scoped token that merely needs replaying against one API is an authentication challenge. The distinguishing feature here is that the material must be transformed — renewed, re-audienced, imported or exchanged — before it opens the target.

external_references.description: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CLD-009 - Redeem and replay delegated cloud tokens
objects.description: The artefact must be transformed before it opens anything. Read it, renew it, re-audience it, then prove access with the least-privileged read that still demonstrates the claim. 1. Decode before trusting. Split the material: a three-part base64url blob is a token (read the algorithm, key identifier, then the claims); a JSON document is a cache or a credential file; a bare opaque string is a renewal credential. Record tenant, client, object, user and audience — the audience is the whole puzzle. 2. Fix the tenant and the client. Both appear in the claims; a tenant identifier in the prompt may be a domain rather than a GUID, so resolve it through the identity provider's metadata document before any request. 3. Renew. Exchange a refresh token at the token endpoint for the resource you actually need, asking for the resource's default scope. An expired access token is not a dead credential when a renewal credential accompanies it. 4. Re-audience. One session can usually mint tokens for several first-party resources. Walk the candidate resources from the story (management plane, graph directory, storage data plane, vault data plane, the challenge's own service) rather than guessing scopes blindly. 5. Complete the flow when a code is supplied. Redeem the code exactly as delivered — the code is single-use and short-lived, so capture the response verbatim, including the renewal credential. 6. Import session material when that is the form given. Cookie or primary-refresh-token material has to be placed where a client expects it before the endpoint accepts it; do the import in a throwaway profile and keep the artefact untouched. 7. Prove the claim narrowly. One read that only the target identity can perform — the directory object of the signed-in principal, the subscription list, the object named in the story — is evidence; a full dump is not. Signatures to expect: a token response with a renewal credential despite no password; a claim set whose audience names the plane the story implied; a refusal that changes with the audience rather than with the identity; a code redemption that reports the grant type the client is allowed; an assertion exchange that fails only because the federation subject does not match.

objects.name: CTFTTE-CLD-010 - Secret store reachable by a workload identity
objects.description: The objective is a value inside a managed secret store — a vault secret, a certificate, a key, a parameter — and the identity the player already holds carries a data-plane grant to it. Nothing has to be broken: the flag is behind a read that the configuration intends to be routine, and the work is to find which store, which object and which version the identity actually reaches. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Grant without discovery. The identity can read the store but holds no listing permission, so object names must be guessed from the narrative, from a leaked template, or from conventional names. - Dual authorisation models. The store accepts both a role-assignment model and a legacy per-object access-policy model; the identity is granted through the one the player does not think to check, so an empty role assignment list is not evidence of denial. - Version history. The current value is a decoy or blank while a previous version still holds the answer; only reading the version list exposes it. - Soft-deleted object. The object was deleted and remains recoverable while purge protection keeps it restorable — the store answers "gone" to a naive read and "still here" to a recovery-aware one. - Object kind mismatch. The answer sits in a certificate or a key, while the player searches secrets only. - Store reached from a workload. The grant belongs to the workload's identity, not the human one, so the token must first come from the instance metadata or the workload's own credential chain. Boundary: when the identity reaches the store through an over-broad administrative role over the whole subscription, the pair is the over-permissive-role one; when the material is a bearer credential embedded in a URL, it belongs to the signed-URL pair. Here the grant is narrow, deliberate and data-plane.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CLD-010 - Enumerate secret stores the held identity can read
objects.description: Treat the identity as the discovery tool: ask the control plane which stores exist, ask the store's own data plane which objects the identity may read, and reconcile the two answers — they are granted through different models and disagree often. 1. Establish which identity you are, from which plane. A human session, a workload identity and an instance-metadata credential reach different stores; resolve the object identifier and the token audience before enumerating. 2. List stores at the control plane. Enumerate the scope you can see for store resources and their recovery settings; note the ones whose name matches the narrative even if the grant looks absent. 3. Check both authorisation models. A data-plane grant may come from a role assignment or from a legacy per-object policy. An empty role-assignment list is not a denial — look for the policy form, and look for grants inherited through a group or a parent scope. 4. Walk object kinds, not just one. Ask for secrets, then keys, then certificates; an empty answer in one kind is routinely filled by another. 5. Read versions and recovery state. Instead the grant travels inside a URL or an artefact as a bearer credential — a signed query string, an account key in a connection string, a delegation key. Whoever holds the string is the principal; no account, no login and no policy edit is required. The author counts on the player discarding the credential as "just a link" or assuming an expired signature means a dead end. Design variants, in increasing subtlety: - Single-object signature. The signature is scoped to one object and no container listing, so the object name has to come from the narrative rather than from enumeration. - Over-broad scope. The signature covers container or account level and several operations, including write or delete, so the exposure exceeds what the story implies. - Expired signature with a live key. The query string is stale, but the account key that produced it is also present in the artefact, and a fresh signature can be computed locally. - Delegation signature. The signature was minted from an identity rather than a key, so re-signing requires a token for that identity — a chain into the session-material pair. - Connection string. The key arrives as a configuration value with a service endpoint, so the player must recognise the format and pick the right client. - Signature in a carrier artefact. The link sits in served HTML, a comment, a mobile bundle or a log line, and only source review surfaces it. objects.name: CTFTTE-CRY-015 - RSA exponent bound by a small linear relation
objects.description: Nothing looks weak: N = p·q is a healthy balanced semiprime, e is full-size, no prime, no bit of d and no helper value is leaked. What is small is not the private exponent but a linear relation the public exponent satisfies: $$e\,x + y \equiv 0 \pmod{\varphi(N)}, \qquad x \approx N^{1/4}, \quad |y| \approx N^{1/8}$$ Every textbook test fails. d is full size, so Wiener (d < N^{1/4}/3) and Boneh-Durfee (d < N^{0.292}) return nothing, Fermat/Pollard never apply, and RsaCtfTool reports "no attack succeeded" because none of its modules test a bounded (x, y) relation. The trap is that the weakness lives in the shape of the exponent pair, invisible to a scanner looking at d alone. The canonical generator is the Yen-Kim-Lim-Moon exponentiation scheme, published as a countermeasure to CRT fault attacks. With φ = φ(N) and a quarter-size bound B = 2^{nbits/4}: er, r ← [1, B] # two small secrets dr = er⁻¹ mod φ d = dr + r # full-size "perturbed" private exponent e = d⁻¹ mod φ # full-size public exponent d is dr plus a 256-bit noise, so it never enters a small-d window. Multiplying e·(dr + r) ≡ 1 by er collapses the construction into the relation above: $$e\,\underbrace{(1 + er r)}{x \approx N^{1/4}} \;\underbrace{- er}{y \approx N^{1/8}} \equiv 0 \pmod{\varphi(N)}$$ Two publication variants: - Parameters published. er and r are printed next to N, e, c. The relation is then immediately evaluable: kφ(N) = e(1 + er·r) − er is a multiple of the totient, and d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod kφ(N)) decrypts — a multiple of φ is as good as φ itself. - Parameters withheld. Only N, e, c are given. The bounded relation is the sole residue of the construction, and it is exactly the input of the generalized Wiener attack (Nitaj, PKC 2004), whose Theorem 2 asks for x ≤ ⅓N^{1/4} and |y| ≤ ½cN^{−3/4}ex with c ≤ 1 — satisfied here because er, r = O(N^{1/8}). The same smell appears whenever an author "adds noise" to a modular inverse instead of drawing d fresh, or reuses one small multiplier across several keys: any leak of x (or of a multiple of φ, see CTFTCTE-CRY-001) plus a small y reopens this relation.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-CRY-015 - Recover the factors from a bounded exponent relation
objects.description: Given N, e (and c), recover φ(N) — or the factors — from e·x + y ≡ 0 (mod φ) with small x, y. Two branches, cheapest first. Branch A — the small parameters are published (er, r given). Evaluate the relation directly; it is a multiple of the totient, and a multiple of φ is enough: kphi = e (1 + er r) - er # == k φ(N) d = inverse(e, kphi) # valid mod kφ, hence mod φ m = pow(c, d, N) Validate with pow(m, e, N) == c, never with the flag format alone. Branch B — only N, e, c are published (generalized Wiener). x sits at the edge of the convergent denominators of e/N, so continued fractions enumerate it: 1. Compute the convergents of e/N — and, when they do not close, their semiconvergents (h{i-1} + j·h{i-2}) / (k{i-1} + j·k{i-2}), because x sits between two convergents as soon as it nears the N^{1/4} edge of the window. 2. For each candidate k/x, s = N + 1 − ⌊e·x / k⌋ estimates p + q; t = s² − 4N estimates (p − q)². 3. If t is a perfect square (search a ±2 window around s to absorb the flooring error), then p = (s + t^{1/2})/2 and N mod p == 0 closes the branch. 4. Otherwise p̃ = (s + ⌊t^{1/2}⌋)/2 is within N^{1/4} of the true prime: Coppersmith f(X) = p̃ + X with X = N^{1/4}, plus the small shifts (2j+1)·N^{1/4} that recentre the unknown, and keep any root that divides N. 5. d = e⁻¹ mod φ, decrypt, re-encrypt to confirm. Expected cost: milliseconds for branch A, under a second for branch B on replayed instances of this construction. The fraction sweep — convergents first, then their semiconvergents — closes roughly nine instances out of ten directly. The residual failures are exactly the instances where x > N^{1/4}/3, i.e. where the theorem's own hypothesis fails: past that edge neither the fraction sweep nor the p̃ + X route is guaranteed, and the next move is a bivariate lattice on the relation itself. Do not read the fallback as dead code. What fails and must not be retried. Wiener (d is full size), Boneh-Durfee (d > N^{0.292}), Fermat (primes are independent and balanced), Pollard p−1, and every automated sweep that only looks at d. Recognising that the weakness is in (x, y), not in d, is the whole solve.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-007 - BLE GATT characteristic gating (pairing / passkey / MAC allow-list / password)
objects.description: The flag sits inside a BLE GATT characteristic reachable only after clearing a client-side gate, not by sniffing the air. Typical gates (as in BLE CTF Infinity): the flag handle is read only after writing a selector to another handle; the peripheral requires BLE pairing with a passkey; it bonds only to a specific BDADDR (MAC allow-list); or it releases the flag only after the correct password is written into a characteristic. The challenge is GATT interaction and its authentication, distinct from IOT-005 (sniffing/decoding the device radio) and from SDR RF puzzles.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-007 - Enumerate and drive BLE GATT as a client
objects.description: Act as a GATT client against the peripheral: bash # 1. Scan / connect and enumerate services, characteristics and handles bettercap -eval "ble.recon on; ble.show" # or: ble.enum <MAC> gatttool -b <MAC> --characteristics # list char handles + properties + UUIDs # 2. Read / write a characteristic by handle (values are hex) gatttool -b <MAC> --char-read -a 0x0016 | awk -F': ' '{print $2}' | xxd -r -p gatttool -b <MAC> --char-write-req -a 0x002e -n $(echo -n "deadbeef" | xxd -ps) # 3. Pair when the peripheral requires a passkey bluetoothctl # agent KeyboardOnly; default-agent; scan on; pair <MAC> # 4. Spoof the local BDADDR for a MAC allow-list gate sudo btmgmt power off; sudo btmgmt public-addr 11:22:33:44:55:66; sudo btmgmt power on # 5. Brute force a 6-digit passkey, or a characteristic password (wordlist, e.g. rockyou.txt) Inspect advertisements and notifications with nRF Connect; analyse a provided BLE PCAP in Wireshark (btatt/btgatt filters). The write-then-read handle pattern (write a selector/password, read the flag handle) is the core loop.

objects.name: CTFTTE-MOB-009 - Engine bytecode packaged with a mobile application
objects.description: The target ships as a mobile application package in which no file holds the logic in the form the platform tooling reads. The decompiled Java/Kotlin layer is a generated shell, the native libraries are the framework's own runtimes, and the application code lives in an asset compiled for the embedded script engine. Nothing is obfuscated: the code is written in a language the platform decompiler does not target, inside a container that makes it look like ordinary mobile code. The concealment is a delivery decision, not a crypto or packing trick, so the failure mode is tooling-shaped: the standard decompiler opens the package, shows a few dozen generated classes, and concludes there is nothing to analyse. What turns it into a technique — and distinguishes it from the sibling bytecode pairs — is the triage the solver has to perform before any code is readable: 1. locate the asset by container convention (the packaged assets directory on Android, the application bundle inside the iOS payload), not by name guessing; 2. identify the engine and its bytecode version from the asset header, because engine decompilers are version-locked and a mismatched version silently produces garbage; 3. recover structure — the function graph and the source-position/name annotations the compiler retained — then read the observable behaviour out of it. The same shape reproduces with any engine a cross-platform framework embeds: only the magic, the version table and the decompiler change. That is why the class is stated in terms of the engine, not of one framework. Boundary: logic hidden in a native library is the same move with a different substrate and belongs to CTFTTE-MOB-002; an author-designed instruction set is CTFTTE-REV-004; an artifact compiled for the same language as the source is CTFTTE-REV-007; JVM artifacts are CTFTTE-REV-006. And once the logic is readable, the endpoints it reveals are ordinary network/web artefacts — the technique ends where that domain begins.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-MOB-009 - Recover application logic from engine bytecode
objects.description: Recover the application's observable behaviour from the engine bytecode the package ships. 1. Confirm the container. List the package. A generated platform shell plus a large asset plus an engine runtime library, and nothing of substance in the platform decompilation, is the signature — stop reading the shell. 2. Locate the asset by convention. Packaged assets directory on Android, application bundle on iOS. Framework naming conventions narrow it to one or two files; brute-forcing names is wasted effort. 3. Identify engine and bytecode version from the header. The version pins the decompiler: a decompiler built for another version emits plausible-looking nonsense, which is worse than an error, so check the version against the tool's supported range first. 4. Decompile, then read the restored module graph. Prefer the artifacts the compiler retained — module boundaries and original function names — over raw disassembly; they turn a flat listing into a call graph. 5. Rebuild the behaviour, not just the strings. Base URL(s), endpoint paths, HTTP verbs, headers, serialized payload shapes, and any value the app persists locally. Then decide what the challenge actually asks for: a value stored by the app is not automatically the answer, and a second endpoint often belongs to the next part of a multi-part challenge. 6. Confirm each hypothesis with a single request. The bundle tells you which calls exist; it rarely tells you what the server returns.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-SDR-002 - Line-coded on-off-keyed remote transmission
objects.description: The flag is the payload of a short on-off-keyed (OOK/ASK) burst such as a garage-door remote, key fob or 433/868 MHz sensor. The carrier is only switched on and off, so demodulated audio sounds like clicks and carries no readable content. The bits are line-coded, typically Manchester (each bit is a transition pair), PWM (short/long pulse) or PPM (short/long gap), and framed by a 1010… preamble and a sync word. That doubles the symbol count and hides the byte alignment. The capture usually arrives as raw IQ (.cf32, .cu8) with the carrier off-centre. Distinct from CTFTTE-IOT-005, where the subject is an IoT protocol stack and its pairing keys, and from CTFTTE-SDR-001, where the modulation itself (AM/FM/FSK/PSK/QAM) is the barrier.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-SDR-002 - Slice the envelope into symbols and decode the line code
objects.description: 1. Find the burst carrier in the spectrum. Mix it to 0 Hz and band-limit it to a few times its occupied width. 2. Take the amplitude envelope and threshold it midway between the noise level and the on level to get on/off runs. 3. Split transmissions on long gaps. Recover the symbol unit as the largest length that fits every run as an integer multiple. The symbol rate is 1/unit; the Manchester bit rate is half of that. 4. Choose the line code from the run widths: - only 1–2-unit runs → Manchester; try both pair phases and both conventions (10=1 G.E. Thomas, 01=1 IEEE 802.3); - two pulse widths with a constant period → PWM; - two gap widths → PPM. 5. Byte-align on the end of the 1010… preamble or on the sync word, convert to bytes and search for the flag format. 6. In inspectrum, the equivalent manual route is: cursors over the burst, an amplitude plot, a threshold plot, then extract the symbols and keep every other bit for Manchester. 7. rtl433 -A prints a pulse analysis and a flex decoder (-X) to replay the decode.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

Its sample format, sample rate and centre frequency are not stated, or the extension is misleading. Read with the wrong format, the file looks like noise. With the wrong sample rate, every timing (baud, pulse width, audio pitch) is off by the same factor. Without the centre frequency, the signal cannot be tied to a band or a protocol. The barrier comes before demodulation: the file has to be read correctly first.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-SDR-003 - Fingerprint the IQ format and recover rate and centre
objects.description: 1. Infer the sample format from the bytes: - size divisibility; - byte histogram (uint8 centred on 127.5 → cu8); - plausible float ranges (cf32); - for floats, the count of distinct values (≤ 256 → an 8-bit origin). 2. Load each candidate format in inspectrum or URH. The right one shows clean carriers and bursts; the wrong ones show noise or mirrored images. 3. Recover the sample rate from structure that has a known timing: a standard channel width, a protocol's fixed symbol rate, or round pulse widths. Common RTL-SDR rates are 1.024, 2.048 and 2.4 MS/s. 4. Take the centre frequency from the challenge story, the filename, or the band a recognised protocol must occupy. Record every assumption, because timings and absolute frequencies are only as good as the rate and centre chosen.

objects.name: CTFTTE-WEB-023 - GraphQL introspection disclosure / field-level authorization gap
objects.description: The flag lives in a sensitive field of a hidden GraphQL object (e.g. postPassword on a post with isHidden: true). The list query the UI uses filters hidden objects out, so the application looks complete and innocent — but the GraphQL endpoint accepts schema introspection, which discloses every type and field name, and the single-object query does not re-apply the list-level filter. Introspection turns authorization-by-obscurity into an open book: the schema names the secret, and a direct query by id reads it. The player is steered toward classic web-vuln hunting while the actual path is schema disclosure plus a field-level authorization gap.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-WEB-023 - Introspect the schema and over-fetch hidden fields
objects.description: 1. Find the GraphQL endpoint: page source, /graphql, /api/graphql, .graphql files, or a framework hint (Apollo, GraphiQL landing page). 2. Introspect: POST the schema { types { name fields { name } } } query; if introspection is disabled, fall back to wordlists of field names and error-message suggestions, or clue mining in client bundles. 3. Triage the schema for sensitive field names (password, hidden, secret, token, admin, flag) and for types the UI never renders — graphql-schema-dump.py automates the dump and the highlight. 4. Compare resolvers: query the list (which the UI filters) and the single-object query by id; enumerate ids the list does not return and over-fetch the sensitive fields on them. 5. Validate: the hidden object's sensitive field satisfies the flag format.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.
